items.stem: A postpartum client receiving a continuous intravenous magnesium sulfate infusion for preeclampsia with severe features develops loss of deep tendon reflexes and respiratory depression. According to maternity nursing practice standards for magnesium toxicity, what should the nurse do first?

options.text: Continue the infusion at the same rate and reassess reflexes in 1 hour.
Stop the magnesium sulfate infusion immediately and notify the health-care provider.
Increase the infusion rate to deepen the anticonvulsant effect.
Administer an additional 4 g magnesium sulfate bolus now.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Continuing the infusion when toxicity signs (absent reflexes, respiratory depression) are present allows magnesium levels to rise further.
rationales.B: Correct. OpenStax directs the nurse to stop the magnesium infusion immediately and notify the provider when toxicity signs appear (loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression); Merck likewise treats significant magnesium toxicity symptoms with calcium gluconate after recognizing toxic levels.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Increasing the rate would worsen magnesium toxicity.
rationales.D: Incorrect. An additional bolus is used for seizure prevention/treatment dosing, not when toxicity is already evident.

items.stem: A labouring client with preeclampsia with severe features is receiving intravenous magnesium sulfate. The nurse notes absent deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate 10/min, and oxygen saturation 89% on room air. For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated at this time.

rows.text: Stop the magnesium sulfate infusion immediately.
Notify the health-care provider of the toxicity findings.
Ensure calcium gluconate is available and administer as ordered.
Increase the magnesium sulfate infusion rate to deepen neuromuscular blockade.
Draw a serum magnesium level as directed after stopping the infusion.

rationales.R1: Indicated. OpenStax lists stopping the infusion immediately as the first response to magnesium toxicity signs such as decreased deep tendon reflexes and respiratory depression.
rationales.R2: Indicated. The provider must be notified promptly when toxicity signs appear so antidote therapy and further orders can be given.
rationales.R3: Indicated. OpenStax identifies calcium gluconate as the antidote that should be accessible (usually at the bedside) and administered as ordered; Merck supports calcium gluconate IV for significant magnesium toxicity symptoms.
rationales.R4: Not indicated. Increasing the infusion would worsen toxicity and is opposite to the required action.
rationales.R5: Indicated. OpenStax directs the nurse to draw a magnesium level immediately after stopping the infusion as part of the toxicity response.

items.stem: A client at 34 weeks’ gestation with known preeclampsia reports a new severe headache and blurred vision. What is the nurse’s priority action?

options.text: Reassure the client that headache is common in late pregnancy and document the report.
Encourage ambulation in the hallway to relieve tension headache.
Notify the health-care provider promptly of possible worsening preeclampsia with severe features.
Delay assessment until the next scheduled prenatal visit in 1 week.

rationales.A: Incorrect. New severe headache with visual change is a warning sign of severe-feature preeclampsia, not a benign late-pregnancy complaint to only document.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Ambulation does not address evolving neurologic end-organ involvement and may delay needed evaluation.
rationales.C: Correct. OpenStax and Merck identify severe headache and visual disturbances as features of preeclampsia with severe features that require prompt recognition and reporting so seizure prevention and delivery decisions can be made.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Waiting a week risks progression to eclampsia or other organ injury.

items.stem: A breastfeeding client at 3 weeks postpartum has unilateral breast erythema, warmth, and tenderness with fever. The provider diagnoses mastitis and starts oral antistaphylococcal antibiotics. Which teaching is most appropriate?

options.text: Stop breastfeeding immediately and wean permanently to prevent spreading infection to the infant.
Continue breastfeeding and/or pumping to empty the affected breast during treatment.
Apply ice packs only and avoid emptying the breast until the fever resolves.
Bind both breasts tightly and withhold feeds for 48 hours.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Merck states breastfeeding and/or pumping should continue during treatment because emptying the affected breast is part of therapy.
rationales.B: Correct. Merck and WHO identify effective emptying of the affected breast—continuing breastfeeding and/or expressing/pumping—as essential treatment; stopping breastfeeding is not required for therapy.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Avoiding emptying promotes engorgement and works against recommended therapy.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Binding and withholding feeds are not recommended management for mastitis.

items.topic: Mastitis — continue breastfeeding/pumping to empty the affected breast

sources.title: Mastitis
sources.evidence: Complete emptying of breast milk; breastfeeding and/or pumping should be continued during treatment.

sources.evidence: Effective milk removal is the most essential part of treatment; encourage frequent breastfeeding; reassure it is safe to continue.

items.stem: Parents of a 6-week-old infant ask how their child should ride in the family vehicle. Which instruction is most appropriate?

options.text: Place the infant in a forward-facing seat with a lap belt only in the front passenger seat.
Use a rear-facing car seat installed in the back seat according to the manufacturer’s limits.
Hold the infant securely on an adult’s lap if the trip is shorter than 30 minutes.
Use an adult seat belt alone because infants under 3 months do not need a car seat.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Infants must ride rear-facing; the front seat is not the safest location for young children.
rationales.B: Correct. Canadian Paediatric Society Caring for Kids and NHTSA both state infants should use a rear-facing car seat and remain rear-facing as long as they fit the manufacturer’s height and weight limits; the back seat is safest.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Holding an infant on a lap does not provide crash protection.
rationales.D: Incorrect. All infants require an appropriate child restraint; adult belts alone are unsafe.

items.stem: An alert 18-month-old with gastroenteritis has mild to moderate dehydration, is able to drink, and has no signs of shock. Which fluid plan is most appropriate initially?

options.text: Immediate intravenous isotonic fluid boluses as first-line therapy for all mild dehydration.
Oral rehydration solution in frequent small amounts, reserving IV fluids for severe dehydration or inability to take oral fluids.
Undiluted fruit juice ad libitum as the preferred rehydration fluid.
Nothing by mouth for 12 hours to rest the bowel before any fluids.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Merck and CDC recommend oral rehydration for mild to moderate dehydration; IV is for severe dehydration or when oral intake is not possible.
rationales.B: Correct. AAP/WHO/Merck and CDC guidance support oral rehydration therapy for mild to moderate dehydration when the child can take fluids orally; severe dehydration with circulatory compromise needs IV fluids.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Commercial ORS with appropriate glucose–sodium composition is preferred over high-sugar juices that can worsen diarrhea.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Gut rest with prolonged NPO is not recommended; rehydration and early feeding are preferred.

items.topic: Pediatric mild–moderate dehydration — oral rehydration first

sources.title: Dehydration in Children
sources.evidence: AAP and WHO recommend oral rehydration for mild and moderate dehydration; children with severe dehydration should receive fluids IV.

sources.title: Managing Acute Gastroenteritis Among Children: Oral Rehydration, Maintenance, and Nutritional Therapy
sources.publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
sources.section: Acute Gastroenteritis Therapy Based on Degree of Dehydration

items.stem: An otherwise healthy 8-month-old is diagnosed with typical viral bronchiolitis. Which statement best reflects evidence-based management?

options.text: Routine nebulized salbutamol should be given to every wheezing infant with bronchiolitis.
Management is primarily supportive (hydration, gentle nasal suctioning, oxygen if needed); routine salbutamol is not recommended when the diagnosis is clear.
Systemic corticosteroids are first-line therapy to shorten every hospital stay.
Chest physiotherapy with percussion is required for all admitted infants.

rationales.A: Incorrect. CPS states that when bronchiolitis diagnosis is clear, a trial of salbutamol is not recommended; Merck notes bronchodilators are not uniformly effective.
rationales.B: Correct. CPS and Merck describe supportive care as the mainstay (hydration, oxygen as needed, comfort measures); CPS explicitly does not recommend routine salbutamol for clear bronchiolitis.
rationales.C: Incorrect. CPS states corticosteroids are not recommended for routine use in bronchiolitis.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CPS states chest physiotherapy is not recommended for bronchiolitis treatment.

items.topic: Bronchiolitis — supportive care; no routine salbutamol
items.jurisdiction_note: CPS (Canada) and Merck (general) concord that care is primarily supportive and bronchodilators are not routinely effective/recommended in typical bronchiolitis.

sources.title: Bronchiolitis: Recommendations for diagnosis, monitoring and management of children one to 24 months
sources.evidence: Management primarily supportive; when diagnosis of bronchiolitis is clear, a trial of salbutamol is not recommended.

sources.title: Bronchiolitis
sources.evidence: Treatment is usually supportive; oxygen and IV hydration as needed; bronchodilators are not uniformly effective.

items.stem: A client on a mental health unit becomes increasingly agitated but is not yet physically assaultive. Which nursing approach best reflects the right to least restrictive treatment?

options.text: Apply four-point restraints immediately to prevent any future escalation.
Place the client in locked seclusion as the first intervention.
Attempt de-escalation first (calm communication, reduce stimuli, offer time-out or PRN medication as appropriate) before seclusion or restraint.
Ignore the agitation until violence occurs, then call security only.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Restraint is among the most restrictive measures and is reserved for last resort after less restrictive options fail.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Seclusion is a highly restrictive intervention used when less restrictive measures have not been effective.
rationales.C: Correct. OpenStax requires least restrictive measures first (de-escalation, reduce stimuli, time-out, PRN medication). Merck likewise states seclusion or restraint is a last resort after lesser restrictive interventions have been attempted.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Early intervention with least restrictive strategies is required; waiting for violence is unsafe and not therapeutic.

items.topic: Aggression — least restrictive alternatives before seclusion/restraint
items.jurisdiction_note: Least-restrictive principles are general; Ontario also has Patient Restraints Minimization Act for hospital restraints (tested separately).

sources.evidence: Providers must use the least restrictive measures that are safe; seclusion/restraint are last resort for severe agitation.

sources.title: Behavioral Emergencies
sources.section: Seclusion or Physical Restraints / Potentially violent patients

items.stem: A young adult starts a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) for major depressive disorder and asks when to expect full benefit. Which teaching is most accurate?

options.text: Full therapeutic effects are usually immediate within the first dose.
Effects may begin in about 2 weeks, with full therapeutic effects often by 4 to 6 weeks; report worsening depression or suicidal thoughts promptly.
If mood is not fully improved by day 3, stop the medication without contacting the provider.
SSRIs never require monitoring for mood changes after starting therapy.

rationales.A: Incorrect. OpenStax and Merck indicate antidepressant benefit is delayed, not immediate after one dose.
rationales.B: Correct. OpenStax nursing implications state effects may start in about 2 weeks with full effects in 4–6 weeks, and clients must report increased depression or suicidal ideation; Merck notes improvement may not be apparent until after 1 to 4 weeks.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Stopping abruptly without guidance is unsafe; delayed onset is expected and the provider should be contacted for concerns.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Antidepressants require monitoring for worsening mood and suicidality, especially in younger clients.

items.topic: SSRI/antidepressant — delayed onset; monitor for worsening mood/suicidality

sources.evidence: These drugs can take 2 weeks to start seeing effects and 4–6 weeks for full therapeutic effects; notify provider about increased depression or suicidal ideations.

items.stem: A hospitalized client with major depression discloses a specific plan to die by suicide using available bed linens and refuses to leave the room. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Arrange for the client to be placed under observation.
Communicate therapeutically and provide emotional support.
Leave the client alone in the room with the door closed for privacy.
Work to limit access to lethal means as part of the safety plan.
Validate the client’s experiences and feelings.
Withhold all prescribed medications permanently without an order.

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax case guidance includes arranging observation for a client with an active inpatient suicide plan.
rationales.B: Correct. Therapeutic communication and emotional support are core nursing actions for a suicidal client.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Leaving a high-risk client alone reduces observation and safety.
rationales.D: Correct. Limiting access to lethal means is a crucial part of a safety plan.
rationales.E: Correct. Validating experiences and feelings supports engagement and assessment.
rationales.F: Incorrect. Withholding medications without an order is not an appropriate suicide-prevention action and may worsen depression.

items.stem: A community health nurse teaches a caregiver about preventing childhood lead exposure in an older home. Which statement indicates correct understanding of primary prevention?

options.text: Primary prevention means waiting until a blood lead level is high before any environmental action.
The most effective approach is to prevent exposure by controlling or removing lead hazards in the environment before a child is exposed.
Lead in household dust is harmless to toddlers because they do not ingest dust.
Sanding old lead paint without dust control is the preferred way to renovate a child’s bedroom.

rationales.A: Incorrect. That describes delayed secondary action; CDC defines primary prevention as removing hazards before exposure.
rationales.B: Correct. CDC states primary prevention—removing lead hazards before a child is exposed—is the most effective approach; Health Canada likewise emphasizes reducing environmental lead exposure and safely managing lead paint/dust risks for children.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Health Canada notes babies and small children can ingest household dust through mouthing behaviours.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Health Canada warns mechanical removal/sanding can release hazardous lead dust and should be avoided.

items.topic: Childhood lead — primary prevention by removing environmental hazards
items.jurisdiction_note: CDC primary-prevention framing and Health Canada lead exposure reduction/safe paint management are concordant on preventing childhood exposure.

sources.evidence: Primary prevention is the removal of lead hazards from the environment before a child is lead exposed; most effective approach.

items.stem: A nurse is teaching a client on day 1 after a vaginal birth about reducing uterine afterpains and keeping the fundus firm. Which instruction is most appropriate?

options.text: Limit fluid intake so the bladder stays full to cushion the uterus.
Empty the bladder often because a full bladder can displace the uterus and increase cramping.
Avoid breastfeeding for 48 hours to prevent oxytocin release.
Remain on complete bed rest without ambulating to the bathroom.

rationales.A: Incorrect. A full bladder displaces the uterus and worsens afterpains; fluids should not be limited for that purpose.
rationales.B: Correct. OpenStax teaches that a full bladder displaces the uterus, requiring stronger contractions to stay firm and increasing pain; frequent emptying is encouraged. Merck notes early postpartum uterine afterpains during involution.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Breastfeeding-related oxytocin supports involution; avoiding feeding is not appropriate teaching for afterpain control.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Clients need to void; preventing bathroom access promotes bladder distention.

items.topic: Postpartum — empty bladder often to prevent uterine displacement and afterpains

sources.title: 20.3 Nursing Care During the Postpartum Period
sources.evidence: Encourage the postpartum person to empty their bladder often; a full bladder displaces the uterus, causing it to contract more to stay firm.

sources.title: Postpartum Care
sources.evidence: During the first few days postpartum, contractions of the involuting uterus may be painful (afterpains) and may require analgesics.
